queue.title: How to Bend Cable Tray Without a Bending Machine
queue.description:
No cable tray bending machine? No problem! ⚡

In this video, I demonstrate a simple method for producing a 90° internal bend in cable tray without using a dedicated cable tray bending machine or a factory-made bend.

Using nothing more than a simple bar with a groove cut into it with a hacksaw, I show how a controlled in-and-out crimping technique can gradually form the tray into a professional-looking 90° internal bend.

This could be particularly useful when you're on a construction site and need to fabricate an internal bend but don't have access to a bending machine or time to wait for a wholesaler to deliver one.

The great thing about this method is the control it gives you over the bending radius. Smaller, gentler crimps can create a more gradual bend, while increasing the amount of movement in each crimp can produce a tighter radius.

A simple bit of site ingenuity that could get you out of trouble on a Friday afternoon! 🛠️⚡

⚡ In this video:
• Making a 90° internal cable tray bend
• Bending tray without a bending machine
• Simple cable tray crimping technique
• Controlling the internal bending radius
• Comparing hand-formed and machine-formed bends
• Practical electrical installation tips

queue.title: There Are a Few Issues With This Heat Pump…
queue.description:
In this video, we take a closer look at an air source heat pump (ASHP) installation and explore some of the important electrical considerations electricians need to understand.

We start with the basic principle of how an air source heat pump works. Much like a refrigerator operating in reverse, a heat pump moves heat rather than simply converting electrical energy directly into heat. This gives us a significant mechanical advantage, with the potential to deliver several units of heat energy for every unit of electrical energy consumed.

We take a look at the unit's energy efficiency rating, noise level and refrigerant before moving on to the part we're particularly interested in the electrical installation.

Following the cabling into the property, we look at how the supply feeds the heat pump controls and consumer unit. We also spot a potential issue with maintaining the required IP4X protection on the top surface of an electrical enclosure.

Then we get to one of the most important points in the video: RCD selection for an air source heat pump.

This particular circuit is protected by a 20 A Type B circuit breaker, but the RCD protection is provided by a Type AC RCCB. Modern heat pumps contain power electronic equipment such as inverter drives, meaning the correct RCD type must be selected in accordance with the equipment manufacturer's instructions.

Depending on the particular heat pump and manufacturer's requirements, this could require Type A, Type F or Type B RCD protection rather than Type AC.

This becomes particularly important when carrying out an Electrical Installation Condition Report (EICR). Identifying the equipment being supplied and checking the manufacturer's requirements can be essential when determining whether the existing RCD protection is suitable.

In this video:

⚡ How an air source heat pump works
⚡ Heat pump efficiency explained
⚡ Electrical input vs heat output
⚡ Energy efficiency ratings
⚡ Heat pump noise levels
⚡ Refrigerants and electrical isolator positioning
⚡ Heat pump electrical supplies
⚡ IP4X requirements for electrical enclosures
⚡ 20 A Type B circuit breaker protection
⚡ Type AC RCD concerns
⚡ Type A, Type F and Type B RCD protection
⚡ Manufacturer's instructions and RCD selection
⚡ What electricians should check during an EICR

As air source heat pumps become increasingly common in UK properties, understanding their electrical requirements — particularly RCD selection and protection — is becoming an important skill for electricians, apprentices and electrical learners.

⚠️ Always consult the equipment manufacturer's current installation instructions and BS 7671 when designing, installing, inspecting or altering electrical installations.

queue.title: Basket weave 12x24 Tile, here's how, and what can go wrong. #tile #basketweave
queue.description:
SUBSCRIBE Learn how to tile the right way.
Basket weave 12x24 Tile, here's how, and what can go wrong. Basket Weave, Double stacked or basket Pattern, not exactly sure what the pattern is called. This is a time lapse of a 12"x 24" Rectified Modular large format porcelain tile installed on Schluter Ditra XL uncoupling membrane
The Tile Pattern consists of two tiles stacked and turned in alternate directions to form large squares of two tiles each. The tiles used to create this pattern must either be modular or have the long side exactly equal to twice the short side including the appropriate grout line width. The tiles in this video were Modular, and also rectified to allow for a very narrow grout line. Generally, cheaper tiles with poor calibration will be difficult to install in a pattern as it will be difficult to keep them  aligned, causing the corners of the tile to run off and result in an unappealing outcome with mismatched corners. It is of critical importance to keep the tiles straight and square to not run into problems with fitting the tiles into the pattern. queue.title: Can You Put a Socket in a Bathroom?
queue.description:
Have we finally found a bathroom big enough to install a BS 1363 13 A socket outlet? At first glance, this enormous bathroom looks like it could be the perfect example but there’s a catch!

In this video, I take a practical look at BS 7671 bathroom zones and the requirements for installing socket outlets in locations containing a bath or shower.

We start by looking at two light fittings positioned alongside the bath. They might initially appear to be within Zone 1, but measuring from the edge of the bath shows that they're actually positioned right at the beginning of Zone 2 – 600 mm from the boundary of Zone 1.

Then we move on to the big question: can we install a standard 13 A socket outlet in this bathroom?

With such a large floor area, it initially appears possible to find a position that's at least 2.5 metres horizontally from the boundary of Zone 1. That could potentially provide a convenient socket near the mirrors for equipment such as a hair dryer.

We also discuss a common misconception surrounding bathroom sinks and basins. The restrictions we're looking at relate to the defined bathroom zones around the bath and shower, rather than simply measuring a distance from a wash basin.

Everything seems promising… until we discover the bathroom also contains a separate shower!

The shower creates another Zone 1 boundary and therefore another 2.5 metre restriction for a socket outlet. Once both the bath and shower are considered, the available distances overlap and every potential position we identified for the socket is ruled out.

So despite the enormous size of this bathroom, the answer is still NO – we can't install the BS 1363 socket outlet in the positions considered.

In this video:

⚡ Bathroom zones explained
⚡ Zone 1 and Zone 2 requirements
⚡ The 600 mm Zone 2 measurement
⚡ BS 1363 socket outlets in bathrooms
⚡ The 2.5 metre requirement explained
⚡ Measuring from the boundary of Zone 1
⚡ Do bathroom sinks create electrical zones?
⚡ Socket outlets near wash basins
⚡ How a separate shower changes the calculation
⚡ Understanding multiple Zone 1 boundaries
⚡ Practical application of BS 7671

A great practical example for electricians, electrical apprentices and learners studying BS 7671 and electrical installations in locations containing a bath or shower.

⚠️ Always refer to the current edition of BS 7671 and applicable manufacturer's instructions when designing or carrying out electrical installations.
